BACKPORT: FROMGIT: LSM: generalize flag passing to security_capable This patch provides a general mechanism for passing flags to the security_capable LSM hook. It replaces the specific 'audit' flag that is used to tell security_capable whether it should log an audit message for the given capability check. The reason for generalizing this flag passing is so we can add an additional flag that signifies whether security_capable is being called by a setid syscall (which is needed by the proposed SafeSetID LSM). Reason for BACKPORT label: aa_capable() function in security/apparmor/capability.c had slightly different logical operator in 4.14. vs latest upstream code. There is no logical difference between the two. Also, change code in security/chromiumos/lsm.c to take advantage of opts arg in security_capable. This allows to refrain from checking the current syscall number when seeing if security_capable is being called from a setid syscall in the chromiumos LSM. BACKPORT: FROMGIT: LSM: add SafeSetID module that gates setid calls SafeSetID gates the setid family of syscalls to restrict UID/GID transitions from a given UID/GID to only those approved by a system-wide whitelist. These restrictions also prohibit the given UIDs/GIDs from obtaining auxiliary privileges associated with CAP_SET{U/G}ID, such as allowing a user to set up user namespace UID mappings. For now, only gating the set*uid family of syscalls is supported, with support for set*gid coming in a future patch set. Reason for BACKPORT label: defining/registering an LSM is slightly different in 4.14 than it is in the latest upstream code. motion_sense: send ODR events to the AP This commits enables the EC to send a motion sense event to the AP when a sensor's ODR is changed. This is done in a way that is backwards compatible on the AP side, in order to enable previous kernels to continue to work (albeit at a loss of new functionality) with up-to-date ECs. Since clients are not required to use a FLUSH when changing ODR, it is possible for the sensor ring to get in a state where it is spreading based on out-of-date delay information, which we observed leading to spreading of overly large intervals, and thus too far into the future. This patch ameliorates that by causing an ODR change to implicitly flush the batching history. CHROMIUM: arm64: dts: rockchip: move scarlet BT wake into USB node QCA6174A's BT wake pin is used on Scarlet, rather than in-band USB wake, to save on power consumption in S3. Currently, we don't coordinate BT activity with our handling of this wakeup pin and just use gpio-keys. That causes problems though, because we have no way of distinguishing wake activity due to a BT device (e.g., mouse) vs. the BT controller (e.g., re-configuring wake mask before suspend). This causes spurious wake events, especially when we add new suspend-time activity in CL:1381326. We can avoid these synchronization problems by handling the BT wake pin directly in the btusb driver -- for all activity up until BT controller suspend(), we simply listen to normal USB activity (e.g., to know the difference between device and host activity); once we're really ready to suspend the host controller, there should be no more host activity, and only *then* do we unmask the GPIO interrupt. List 2 compatible properties, since both PID/VID pairs show up on Scarlet devices, and they're both essentially identical QCA6174A-based modules. Also note that the polarity was wrong before: Qualcomm implemented WAKE as active high, not active low. We only got away with this because gpio-keys always reconfigured us as bi-directional edge-triggered. We have an external pull-up and a level-shifter on this line, so we can't do pull-down. Switch to pull-none. This change was also sent upstream, but the DTS structure is fairly different there: https://lore.kernel.org/patchwork/patch/1045207/ https://lkml.kernel.org/r/20190222225345.69084-3-briannorris@chromium.org BUG=chromium:934130 TEST=suspend_stress_test (w/ or w/o BT device), see no spurious wake TEST=revert CL:1454323 and do above test TEST=BT wake with BT HID device Change-Id: I81ce9edb71d7e35f3c3c863c8cd483f393687b7d Signed-off-by: Brian Norris <briannorris@chromium.org> Reviewed-on: https://chromium-review.googlesource.com/1481914

sepolicy: add type_transistion when chromeos_domain creating under /var Use type_transistion to make sure creating directory "lib" under any directory labelled as cros_var are automatically labelled as cros_var_lib, and vice-versa for "cache", "log", etc. Directories under /var/ like /var/lib, /var/spool, may be deleted and re-created during running of the system, including tests. Previously, we have `restorecon -R -D /var` to fixing SELinux file labels under /var upon boot. But `-D` options makes it only tries to fix when the policy has changed, for example, policy upgrades along with OTA. Recreated /var/lib won't be "fixed" upon any reboot unless the policy has changed. The major reason for not to attempt relabelling everytime is recursive relabelling takes time, and this will slow down Chrome OS boot process. Also, relabelling shouldn't be necessary unless the policy has changed if everything is functioning well. moblab-generic-vm-paladin provision_AutoUpdate has encourterd the situation that after AutoUpdate, files under /var/lib including /var/lib itself is not correctly labeled, because there's no policy upgrade. restorecon simply skips everything to not to slow down boot process with a recursive relabelling, which does nothing most of the time. crrev.com/c/1450654 provides an emergency workaround "fix" like `restorecon -R -D /var/*` which expands to `retorecon -R -D /var/lib /var/cache /var/log ...`, since the last policy is stored at the xattr of the specified directory inode, recreated /var/lib will be treated as relabeling needed since no last policy hash is stored at /var/lib, but only at /var. type_transistion will be the long term fix to let kernel correctly recreate the directory with correct label, and leaving `restorecon -R -D /var` for policy upgrades, or first policy introduction purpose only. python2: use PGO on the interpreter This CL turns on PGO for all builds of Python's interpreter. Python appears to have support for some of this on its own, though: - that support appears to be confined to GCC in Python2 (Python3 grew support for clang at some point) - for reasons detailed below, we don't want to generate a new profile on every `emerge` of Python ...So none of that is really useful to us in Python2. PGO increases the installed tree size by 8KB, so size isn't an issue here. Experimentally, PGO makes Python-heavy operations (such as `equery b /path/to/foo`) consume 8% fewer user cycles than builds without PGO. Due to issues with LTO, a comment was added about it, but it wasn't enabled. This also includes a script that can be used to generate new profiles. Since profile generation is nondeterministic, and since it takes O(minutes), we don't regenerate profiles on each run of the ebuild. Given the scary comment at the top of python's ebuild, I added a nop change to dev-install so it's hopefully uprevved. FROMGIT: ath10k: pci: use mutex for diagnostic window CE polling The DIAG copy engine is only used via polling, but it holds a spinlock with softirqs disabled. Each iteration of our read/write loops can theoretically take 20ms (two 10ms timeout loops), and this loop can be run an unbounded number of times while holding the spinlock -- dependent on the request size given by the caller. As of commit 39501ea64116 ("ath10k: download firmware via diag Copy Engine for QCA6174 and QCA9377."), we transfer large chunks of firmware memory using this mechanism. With large enough firmware segments, this becomes an exceedingly long period for disabling soft IRQs. For example, with a 500KiB firmware segment, in testing QCA6174A, I see 200 loop iterations of about 50-100us each, which can total about 10-20ms. In reality, we don't really need to block softirqs for this duration. The DIAG CE is only used in polling mode, and we only need to hold ce_lock to make sure any CE bookkeeping is done without screwing up another CE. Otherwise, we only need to ensure exclusion between ath10k_pci_diag_{read,write}_mem() contexts. This patch moves to use fine-grained locking for the shared ce_lock, while adding a new mutex just to ensure mutual exclusion of diag read/write operations. Tested on QCA6174A, firmware version WLAN.RM.4.4.1-00132-QCARMSWPZ-1. Fixes: 39501ea64116 ("ath10k: download firmware via diag Copy Engine for QCA6174 and QCA9377.") vm_tools: maitred: max stateful fs size at boot As a first step toward more dynamic stateful disk sizing, add a btrfs online resize operation to maximize the filesystem within its block device. This will take place on each boot, but it should have minimal overhead if the block device size has not changed (less than 10 ms) and should not take a significant amount of time even when actually resizing, since this will always be expanding into new free space, which doesn't require any shuffling of existing data (growing a 1 GB FS to 2 GB takes less than 100 ms on my test system). Note that this will only work for expanding the disk image; it is not safe to shrink the disk image unless the filesystem is shrunk first, which will never happen in this code path due to the use of 'max' as the size specifier. The approach taken here is enough to allow the virtual block device image to be resized to let the VM consume newly-available free space that wasn't available at VM creation time. Shrinking the VM disk image would need to issue a BTRFS resize operation with an absolute size specified, followed by shrinking the disk image file to that size. However, since we use a sparse backing file for the stateful disk image, free space should already be reclaimed from the VM even if the logical disk size is larger than the available space. Tested by manually expanding the stateful disk image with truncate(1) and restarting the VM, observing the change in filesystem size. FROMGIT: ath10k: pci: use mutex for diagnostic window CE polling The DIAG copy engine is only used via polling, but it holds a spinlock with softirqs disabled. Each iteration of our read/write loops can theoretically take 20ms (two 10ms timeout loops), and this loop can be run an unbounded number of times while holding the spinlock -- dependent on the request size given by the caller. As of commit 39501ea64116 ("ath10k: download firmware via diag Copy Engine for QCA6174 and QCA9377."), we transfer large chunks of firmware memory using this mechanism. With large enough firmware segments, this becomes an exceedingly long period for disabling soft IRQs. For example, with a 500KiB firmware segment, in testing QCA6174A, I see 200 loop iterations of about 50-100us each, which can total about 10-20ms. In reality, we don't really need to block softirqs for this duration. The DIAG CE is only used in polling mode, and we only need to hold ce_lock to make sure any CE bookkeeping is done without screwing up another CE. Otherwise, we only need to ensure exclusion between ath10k_pci_diag_{read,write}_mem() contexts. This patch moves to use fine-grained locking for the shared ce_lock, while adding a new mutex just to ensure mutual exclusion of diag read/write operations. Tested on QCA6174A, firmware version WLAN.RM.4.4.1-00132-QCARMSWPZ-1. Fixes: 39501ea64116 ("ath10k: download firmware via diag Copy Engine for QCA6174 and QCA9377.")
